text: Gustav Kramer (11 March 1910 – 19 April 1959) was a German zoologist and ornithologist specializing in allometry. He first described Xenopus laevis, the African clawed frog, in his doctoral thesis. In 1933, he conducted a study on Xenopus laevis in Berlin at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Medical Research, where he worked under Ludolf von Krehl on the metabolism of warm-blooded animals. Subsequently, he served as an assistant at the German-Italian Institute of Marine Biology in Rovinj, Croatia. In 1941, he moved to Naples to study lizards, particularly the Adriatic lizard, focusing on the comparative morphological and genetic differences between mainland and island forms to understand speciation. In 1948, he led a department at the Max Planck Institute for Marine Biology in Wilhelmshaven, where he investigated how birds orient themselves over long distances. He developed an apparatus to test how animals respond to the sun's position by misleading them into believing the sun was in a different location, demonstrating that flight direction depends on the sun's position in the sky. Since this ability requires an internal clock to track the time of day, Kramer collaborated with Jürgen Aschoff. From 1 April 1958, he worked with Aschoff at the Max Planck Institute near Tübingen, where he introduced the term Zugunruhe, meaning migratory restlessness. On 19 April 1959, while attempting to remove young rock pigeons from their nests in the mountains of Calabria, he fell and died instantly. His two sons recovered his body from the fast-flowing mountain river Raganello. An obituary by Konrad Lorenz in the Journal of Ornithology noted that Kramer's "authorized worldwide fame as the initiator of experimental analytical orientation research" should not be forgotten.
